procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 29th September, 2023 of the High Court, quashing criminal proceedings.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings without securing the personal presence of the appellant and verifying if there was a settlement.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the appellant argued that the High Court should not have quashed the criminal proceedings without verifying the settlement with the appellant in person. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and order, restored the Criminal Miscellaneous Application to the High Court's file, and directed the High Court to relist the petition before the Roster Bench.

directions: The impugned judgment and order dated 29th September, 2023 is set aside.
Criminal Miscellaneous Application (for quashing and setting aside the FIR/order) No.15041 of 2023 is restored to the file of the High Court.
The restored petition be listed before the Roster Bench before the High Court on 2nd December, 2024 in the morning.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court must satisfy itself that there is a genuine settlement between the victim and the accused before quashing criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences on the ground of settlement.

facts: A petition was filed before the High Court to quash a charge sheet for serious, non-compoundable offences (including under Section 376(2)(N) of the IPC and the Atrocities Act) based on an alleged settlement between the accused and the victim.
The High Court proceeded to quash the criminal proceedings based on this alleged settlement.
law: When a High Court is asked to quash criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences on the basis of a settlement, it has an absolute duty to first satisfy itself that a genuine settlement exists between the victim and the accused.
A petition to quash cannot proceed further until the court is satisfied that the settlement is genuine.

To verify the settlement, especially in serious cases involving women, it is advisable for the High Court to secure the victim's presence, either in person or through video conference, to confirm the settlement is voluntary and that they have no remaining grievances.
Alternatively, the High Court can order an inquiry by a Judicial Officer to determine the genuineness of the settlement.
Even after confirming a genuine settlement, the High Court must still consider whether the nature of the offence is such that quashing the proceedings is appropriate in the interest of justice.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had quashed the criminal proceedings without first verifying whether a genuine settlement actually existed between the victim (appellant) and the accused.
The High Court failed to secure the personal presence of the victim to confirm the details and voluntariness of the alleged settlement.
By not performing this essential verification, the High Court erred in its procedure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that the High Court must satisfy itself that a genuine settlement exists before it can consider quashing criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences. Because the High Court in this case failed to undertake this necessary verification, its order quashing the proceedings was found to be unsustainable and was set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences can be quashed by the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. or Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground of a settlement between the victim and the accused.

facts: A petition was filed before the High Court to quash a charge sheet for serious, non-compoundable offences (including under Section 376(2)(N) of the IPC and the Atrocities Act) on the basis of an alleged settlement between the accused and the victim.
The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings without securing the personal presence of the victim to verify whether a genuine settlement had actually occurred.
law: The High Court has inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) and extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
These powers can be invoked to quash criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice.
application: The Supreme Court established a two-step process for the High Court when considering quashing non-compoundable offences based on a settlement.
First, the High Court must rigorously satisfy itself that a genuine settlement exists between the victim and the accused. An affidavit alone may not be sufficient.

To verify the settlement, especially in serious cases and those involving women, the Court should procure the victim's presence, either in person or through video conferencing, to confirm the settlement is voluntary and that they have no remaining grievances. The Court can also order an inquiry by a Judicial Officer.

Second, only after being satisfied that the settlement is genuine, the High Court must then consider whether it is appropriate to exercise its power to quash the proceedings in the specific facts of the case. This is a discretionary step.
The Court noted that factors like the gruesome nature of the offence and whether it is an offence against society are relevant considerations in this second step.
In the present case, the High Court failed at the first step by quashing the proceedings without verifying the authenticity of the settlement with the victim, rendering its order unsustainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a High Court has the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. or Article 226 of the Constitution to quash criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences based on a settlement. However, this power is conditional. The High Court must first conduct a thorough verification to ensure the settlement is genuine and voluntary, preferably by hearing from the victim directly. If a genuine settlement is confirmed, the court must then exercise its discretion to decide if quashing is appropriate, considering the seriousness and nature of the offence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court must satisfy itself that there is a genuine settlement between the victim and the accused before quashing criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences on the ground of settlement.
appellant_arguments: The High Court failed in its duty to verify if a genuine settlement existed.
The High Court should have secured the appellant's personal presence to confirm the settlement, instead of relying on suspicious affidavits.
The affidavits were unreliable because the appellant is illiterate, and there was no endorsement confirming the contents were explained to her before she put her thumb impression.
The circumstances surrounding the affidavits were suspicious, as one was in English and another in Gujarati, allegedly executed in two different cities (Ahmedabad and Rajkot) on the same day.
It was not clear if the advocate who represented the appellant in the High Court was genuinely authorized by her.
The practice of simply producing affidavits from the victim with the quashing petition is objectionable and insufficient for proper verification.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judgment and order passed by a High Court based on a settlement between parties is unsustainable if the court has not verified whether the settlement was genuine.
obiter: It will always be open for the appellant to file an affidavit before the High Court on the issue of settlement.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: As the High Court has passed the impugned judgment and order without verifying whether there was a genuine settlement between the appellant and the second respondent, the impugned judgment and order cannot be sustained.
legal_tests_applied: Before quashing criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences on the ground of a settlement, the High Court has a duty to actively verify whether a genuine settlement was reached between the victim and the accused.
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court did not rule on the ultimate question of whether the High Court has the power to quash these specific criminal proceedings based on a compromise. Instead, it kept that question open and remanded the case for the High Court to decide after proper verification of the settlement.
policy_considerations: The court addressed the 'objectionable practice' of simply producing affidavits signed by the complainant/victim along with the quashing petition, indicating that such a passive acceptance of documents is an insufficient safeguard to ensure a settlement is genuine.
